extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, merchants, and students of political economy
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive principles and practical guidance on trade policy, import restraints, and banking practices (as argued in an 18th-century political economy treatise). Useful for thinking about how to implement or evaluate trade liberalization, customs policy, and deposit-bank arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore freedom of trade gradually
rubrics_metrics.description: The freedom of trade should be restored only by slow gradations, and with a good deal of reserve and circumspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sudden removal of high duties and prohibitions could flood the home market with cheaper foreign goods and deprive many thousands of people of their ordinary employment and subsistence. Therefore, changes should be introduced slowly, with long warning, to avoid considerable disorder and to allow capital and labour to reallocate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exporting manufactures are little affected by freer importation
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufactures of which any part is commonly exported to other countries (without a bounty) will be little affected by the freest importation of foreign goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such manufactures must be sold as cheaply abroad as foreign competitors of the same quality and so will retain the home market. Examples given: many branches of woollen manufacture, tanned leather, hardware (large employers) versus silk and linen (which may suffer more).

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitate labour mobility and remove internal restraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Permit workers to seek employment in other trades or places by breaking down exclusive privileges and repealing restraints on movement and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically: break down exclusive privileges of corporations, repeal the statute of apprenticeship, and repeal the law of settlements so poor workmen can seek employment elsewhere without fear of prosecution or removal. Analogy: discharged soldiers/seamen found other employment when forces were reduced; manufacturers can more easily transfer their labour to related trades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of political resistance from vested interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Public prejudices and private interests (manufacturers, monopolists) will resist freedom of trade and can intimidate legislature and public officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacturers may mobilize their workmen and influence members of parliament; those who oppose monopolies often face abuse, detraction, personal insults, and sometimes danger from outraged monopolists. Policy reformers must account for entrenched interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce changes with equitable regard for fixed capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislature should respect the equitable interest of manufacturers whose capital is fixed in workhouses and instruments of trade; sudden changes cause loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of an undertaker's capital (materials, wages) may find other employment, but capital fixed in buildings and instruments is hard to dispose of without considerable loss. Therefore, changes affecting such capital should be slow and accompanied by long warning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating or extending monopolies
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislature ought to be particularly careful neither to establish any new monopolies nor to extend those already established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every such regulation introduces some degree of real disorder into the constitution of the state, which will be difficult afterwards to cure without causing another disorder. Monopolies concentrate numbers and wealth that can intimidate government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate taxes for revenue from protectionist duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes upon importation that are intended to raise revenue for government may be proper, but taxes imposed to prevent or diminish importation are destructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxes aimed at preventing imports harm both the customs revenue and the freedom of trade; the author defers detailed tax discussion to another chapter but signals this normative distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary restraints on imports from 'unfavourable-balance' countries are unreasonable
rubrics_metrics.description: Laying extraordinary restraints on goods from countries with which the balance is supposed disadvantageous is an expedient of the commercial system to increase bullion, but is unreasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith offers multiple arguments why such restraints fail even under mercantilist logic: cheaper/better foreign goods can be advantageous, re-exportation can offset imports, and there is no certain criterion to determine true bilateral balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheaper/better foreign goods can be beneficial despite bilateral 'unfavourable' balance
rubrics_metrics.description: If goods from one country (e.g., France) are better and cheaper than those from others, it is more advantageous to purchase from that country even if the bilateral balance seems adverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though the value of annual imports from that country may rise, the value of whole annual importations may fall if cheaper goods substitute for more expensive ones from other countries; consumption and national advantage can increase despite a local increase in import value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-exportation can offset imports and bring returns
rubrics_metrics.description: A portion of imported goods may be re-exported profitably to other countries, bringing back returns equal or superior to the prime cost of the imported goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Dutch trade in carrying French goods to other European countries. Some French wine drunk in Britain may be clandestinely imported through Holland. Engaging in carriage/re-export trade can confer advantages even when direct bilateral trade appears imbalanced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom-house books are an uncertain criterion of balance
rubrics_metrics.description: The custom-house books are a very uncertain criterion for determining balance between countries because of inaccuracies in valuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many goods are misvalued or inaccurately rated in customs returns, so relying on such records to assess whether trade is 'favourable' or 'unfavourable' is misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course of exchange is an unreliable indicator of bilateral trade balance
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary course of exchange between two places does not certainly indicate the balance of their exports and imports because it is influenced by dealings with many other places and by differences in standards/currencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: merchants paying Hamburg via bills on Holland; computed exchange may show one direction while real exchange (accounting for coin wear, coinage costs, bank money) shows another. Therefore exchange rates alone cannot definitively establish a trade surplus or deficit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computed exchange can mislead due to coin quality and mint standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Judging value of current money by mint standards is fallible because circulating coin may be worn, clipped, or degraded, so the computed exchange can differ from the real exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: before English coin reformation, computed exchange with Holland was 25% against England, but English coin was below standard by about that amount so the real exchange might have been in England's favour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coinage costs and bank-money (agio) affect real exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in who bears coinage expense and the existence of bank money (which carries an agio) mean the computed exchange may be biased; bank money is worth more than common currency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In France, an 8% coinage duty increases the value of French coin relative to its nominal silver content; in Amsterdam and other banking centres, bills are paid in bank money which is intrinsically worth more than common currency (agio), affecting perceived exchange relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use banks of deposit (bank money) to reduce exchange uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Small states created banks that pay foreign bills in bank money—credit recorded to a standard—which stabilises the value of bills and removes uncertainty caused by degraded circulating coin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Amsterdam bank (est. 1609) received coin and worn foreign coin, credited accounts in bank money at standard intrinsic value, and mandated payment of large bills in bank money, thereby requiring merchants to maintain bank accounts and providing a secure, transferable medium for international payments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bank practices for bullion deposits and receipts
rubrics_metrics.description: Banks may grant credit upon deposits of bullion at rates somewhat below mint price, issue recipices/receipts convertible into bullion within a fixed term, and charge a keeping fee; unclaimed deposits may become bank property after term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amsterdam bank practice: credit ≈5% below mint price; receipts entitle bearer to withdraw within six months upon reassigning bank money equal to the original credit and paying a keeping fee (¼% for silver, ½% for gold); receipts and bank credit are tradable and serve different functions in commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bank money bears an agio due to convenience and security
rubrics_metrics.description: Bank money commands a premium (agio) over common currency because it is secure, transferable by simple transfer, and trusted by the state backing the bank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages include security from fire/robbery, easy transfer without transportation risk, and standardised intrinsic value; depositors commonly left funds in bank because bank money could be sold at a premium rather than withdrawn and mixed with worn currency.
